newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's first giant copper mine nears startup.
newsitem.headline: Argentina's first giant copper mine nears startup.

text.p: Despite unusual weather and inexperienced bureaucracy, Argentina's first giant copper mine, the $900 million Bajo de la Alumbrera, is nearing completion on schedule, officials said.
The open pit is already being carved out between cactus-dotted mountains in Argentina's northwestern desert, and the world's largest SAG mills have been installed on target for an August start-up.
"The sheer size of the project makes it one hell of a challenge. Technically the project is not particularly complex," said Minera Alumbrera Limited operations general manager Richard Swann.

This is good news for Alumbrera's partners, for whom success of the project is vital. Lead partner MIM Holdings Ltd, which made a small loss in the first half of Australia's 1996/97 financial year, is particularly in need of success at Alumbrera.
MIM's partners are compatriots North Ltd and Canada's Rio Algom Ltd, which each have 25 percent.

"It's seen as a significant step out for all three joint venturers. In terms of capital it's a significant percentage of their capitalization for all three," Alumbrera president Peter Freund told reporters.
Alumbrera should be the world's ninth largest copper mine and is set to produce 190,000 tonnes of copper in concentrates a year, plus 730,000 ounces of gold.
There have been hiccups. Firstly it rained in the desert, overburdening drainage systems. Torrential rains also delayed work on the 240-km slurry pipeline to a filtration plant in Tucuman province.

As the first really big mining project in Argentine history, Alumbrera has had to suffer the teething troubles of a bureacracy willing to help but inexperienced in applying the new rules which have attracted foreign miners to the country in the 1990s, Freund said.
One problem has been delays in refunding value-added tax paid on capital equipment, although Freund said President Carlos Menem had assured him the payments would be made.
Argentina's legal system has also caused some delays in finalizing project finance, particularly due to its exacting requirements for guarantees.
"We don't have the same legal mechanisms to pledge a group of assets. We have to prepare a mortgage for each individual asset," Freund said, adding that the project's legal bill had run over budget.
Another teething test for Alumbrera and Argentine mining is due at the end of the year, when a two-year contract with the mining union comes up for renegotiation.
When operating, the mine will employ about 650 workers, who will mainly earn about $1,000 a month -- a handsome wage in the dusty, economically depressed province of Catamarca.
Others will hope to learn from Alumbrera's Argentine trail-blazing.
Australia's BHP is leading the Agua Rica copper project nearby, and Freund said Alumbrera had had early talks with them about the possibility of sharing infrastructre.
